item.title: Hi-tech Shenzhen takes centre stage as Xi sends ‘Chinamaxxing’ message at Apec summit
item.description:
Crowds gather to watch a light show for the Apec summit in Shenzhen. Photograph: Alex Plavevski/EPA
View image in fullscreen
Crowds gather to watch a light show for the Apec summit in Shenzhen. Photograph: Alex Plavevski/EPA
Hi-tech Shenzhen takes centre stage as Xi sends ‘Chinamaxxing’ message at Apec summit
Host city offers showcase of China’s rise into a confident and innovative power central to global economy
In a Shenzhen square on a balmy evening, locals and tourists watched the dozens of glinting towers that make up the city’s skyline ripple through the colour spectrum – cyan and violet, cyber green, China’s national scarlet and gold – repeatedly flashing the words “Apec 2026”.
The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is a dream showcase for one of China’s most advanced cities, and the country’s leader, Xi Jinping, is basking in its neon glow.
On the sidelines, a series of high-profile bilateral meetings and the announcement of a historic three-way summit with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin have cemented Xi’s status as an agenda setter on the global stage.
The broader Apec summit, meanwhile, provides an opportunity for China to present itself as a steward of multilateralism against what it terms “unilateralism and protectionism” – that is to say, trade measures taken against Beijing by countries such as the US.
View image in fullscreen
A humanoid robot serves a cup of coffee at the Apec media centre in Shenzhen. Photograph: Tingshu Wang/Reuters
All this is set against the futuristic backdrop that is Shenzhen, a city that perhaps better than no other embodies China’s rise into a confident, technologically innovative power central to the global economy.
A photo display in the Apec media centre charts Shenzhen’s transformation from sparsely populated marshland, calling it “a miracle in the history of world development created by the Chinese people”.

item.title: Apec summit live: Xi welcomes Trump on China visit as Putin claims Europe in ‘humiliating decline’ in speech
item.description:
Thanks for tuning into our live blog of the Apec summit currently under way in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.
There is plenty more to come, so don’t go away, but here is a quick summary of what we know so far.
Chinese president Xi Jinping opened the Apec CEO summit on Wednesday with a speech calling for freer trade and greater cooperation around AI. “We should not only eliminate trade and investment barriers... but also promote inclusive and balanced development,” he said. “We should actively build partnerships for scientific and technological innovation, deepen cooperation in the digital economy and artificial intelligence and promote a green and low-carbon transition.”
Russian president Vladimir Putin also addressed the summit, speaking after Ukraine destroyed the vital Kerch road bridge linking occupied Crimea to Russia in a major blow to his four-year-old war. Putin followed Xi on stage with a speech that described Western powers as “former hegemons”. He said Europe was in a “humiliating decline” and that anti-Russian sanctions imposed ⁠after his invasion of Ukraine had backfired, instead making his country stronger.
Xi and Putin headed into a meeting after their opening addresses, according to Chinese and Russian state media.
Russia’s president Vladimir Putin and Chinese president Xi Jinping shake hands prior to a meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen, China. Photograph: Sergei Bobylyov/AFP/Getty Images
The much-anticipated trilateral meeting between US president Donald Trump, Xi and Putin will take place on Thursday. The three men are due to meet on the sidelines and potentially discuss Russia’s war with Ukraine and the US war in Iran, as well as other flashpoints such as trade, ⁠AI and nuclear weapons.

item.title: Trump, Xi and Putin have a shared vision of global power – with no place for Europe | Rafael Behr
item.description:
Donald Trump hosts China’s president, Xi Jinping, at the White House in September 2026. Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
Donald Trump hosts China’s president, Xi Jinping, at the White House in September 2026. Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
Trump, Xi and Putin have a shared vision of global power – with no place for Europe Rafael Behr
In a world carved into continental blocs by authoritarians, Britain has to make common cause with its neighbours
In the chronicles of 21st-century diplomacy few statements have caused as much offence with as few words as Barack Obama’s 2014 description of Russia as a “regional power”.
Vladimir Putin’s politics were defined then, as now, by vengeful resentment of his country’s relegation from superpower status after the cold war. His worldview is warped by a paranoid conviction that Nato never stopped striving to deepen that humiliation, even after the USSR had unravelled. From his Kremlin throne, the Russian president expects to be treated as a colossus of world history. It is hard to overstate how bitterly he hated being dismissed by Obama as a geopolitical B-lister.
In Donald Trump, Putin has a ready supplier of balm to soothe his injured vanity. The US president has a shallow, venal concept of power. He is impressed by gilded palaces and heavily armed thugs. He feels thwarted by American democracy and envies tyrants who operate without equivalent restraint. Since Trump measures greatness in a country by its leader’s contempt for smaller nations and appetite for self-enriching plunder, he willingly promotes Russia back to the top tier.
That is the significance to Putin of a three-way summit with Trump and China’s Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Thursday. It confers trappings of parity with the world’s two genuine superpowers. That is a win for Russia, regardless of whether anything of substance is agreed.

item.title: Jensen Huang to testify before Congress on ‘potential breach of national security’
item.description:
Jensen Huang on 3 December 2025. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
Jensen Huang on 3 December 2025. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images
Jensen Huang to testify before Congress on ‘potential breach of national security’
High-stakes hearing comes in wake of resignation from Nvidia after alleged affair with suspected Chinese spy
Nvidia’s former CEO Jensen Huang will testify before several congressional committees on 1 December, setting the stage for a high-stakes hearing in the wake of his resignation following an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
Tim Teter, Nvidia’s general counsel, has also agreed to appear for a closed-door transcribed interview the following day, 2 December.
“We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security,” Congressmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford, who chair the committees, said in a press release. “The American people need answers on Mr Huang and Nvidia’s role in allowing dangerous [People’s Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal.”Jensen Huang says he would be ‘honored’ to return to Nvidia as CEO
Read more
The three congressmen chair the foreign affairs committee, the select committee on the Chinese Communist party, and the intelligence committee of the House of Representatives, respectively. On 12 November, they had signed a letter warning Huang that he could face a subpoena if he did not agree to the closed-door meeting.
Nvidia chips are key to powering the artificial intelligence boom. The Trump administration has prohibited the selling of advanced artificial intelligence chips to China.
Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO after allegations of extramarital relationships with the suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang and two Nvidia employees surfaced.

item.title: Jensen Huang’s departure as Nvidia CEO becomes a political proxy war
item.description:
Jensen Huang, the Nvidia CEO and co-founder who resigned last week. Photograph: Chesnot/Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
Jensen Huang, the Nvidia CEO and co-founder who resigned last week. Photograph: Chesnot/Getty Images
Jensen Huang’s departure as Nvidia CEO becomes a political proxy war
Huang’s exit sharpens debate over US stance towards Beijing; and as outages increase, do you get the feeling nothing works?
This was originally published in TechScape, a newsletter about how technology shapes our lives. Sign up to receive it here.
Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m your host, Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you from a plane back from Web Summit in Lisbon. Today in tech, we’re discussing the implications of Jensen Huang’s ouster, and the recent spate of failures in critical infrastructure in everything from Microsoft Outlook accounts to air traffic control to copper wires in routers.
Nvidia’s CEO exit becomes a political proxy war
View image in fullscreen
Photograph: Florence Lo/Reuters
The chief executive officer of what once was the most valuable company in the world resigned on Thursday. Jensen Huang’s departure from chipmaker Nvidia after news broke he had at least three affairs – one with an executive at the datacenter firm Megaspeed, whom US intelligence has investigated for spying for China; others with his own employees – has already cost his company hundreds of billions in stock market value. It may cost the world economy much more. Nvidia is central to the AI boom both as chipmaker and lender.
We’ll know more about the company’s path forward later on Tuesday when it reports its quarterly earnings. Executives, especially interim CEO Colette Kress, will face investors’ questions about the post-Huang era.

item.title: Xi, Trump and Putin to discuss ‘world peace’ at trilateral, says China
item.description:
Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping are scheduled to hold an unprecedented trilateral meeting this Thursday. Photograph: Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping are scheduled to hold an unprecedented trilateral meeting this Thursday. Photograph: Getty Images
Xi, Trump and Putin to discuss ‘world peace’ at trilateral, says China
Beijing stops short of confirming specific agenda, but Trump says denuclearisation, Iran war, trade and Ukraine will be among topics
The meeting of Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen this week will cover topics of “groundbreaking significance” including “safeguarding world peace”, the Chinese foreign ministry has said.
The confirmation of Thursday’s trilateral talks, the first of their kind, will take place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit and cement Xi’s status as a global power broker as he presides over events in the glittering southern tech hub of Shenzhen.
At the White House, Trump told reporters he would be speaking to his Chinese and Russian counterparts about denuclearisation, the war in Iran, economics, trade and “my favourite subject, Ukraine”. US officials had earlier indicated that Trump would not discuss Russia’s war in Ukraine during the trip.
Trump also said he may meet North Korea’s Kim Jong-un in what would be their first meeting of his second term. “We may meet with Kim Jong-un also,” Trump said. “So that will be good … we have a chance to accomplish a lot.”
Asked whether Kim would be there, Trump said that he “may come”. “I don’t know,” he said. “That’s up to president Xi.”
Many, including the UN secretary general, António Guterres, had hoped the trilateral talks would be used to discuss reductions in nuclear arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers.

item.title: Trump to embark on Asia trip in apparent foreign policy push before end of term
item.description:
‘The president has been badly damaged by the election and will have limited prospects for the next two years,’ said one China specialist. Photograph: Evan Vucci/Reuters
View image in fullscreen
‘The president has been badly damaged by the election and will have limited prospects for the next two years,’ said one China specialist. Photograph: Evan Vucci/Reuters
Trump to embark on Asia trip in apparent foreign policy push before end of term
Experts say US president may lean toward global affairs after domestic influence curtailed in midterm elections
Donald Trump is embarking on his first overseas trip since his Republican party’s thumping midterm repudiation by US voters, in what may herald a renewed focus on foreign policy for the remainder of his presidency.
The US president will meet his Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, for their first trilateral summit, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum in the Chinese city of Shenzhen. Before that, he will land in Manila in the Philippines on Tuesday for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit.
At the Asean summit, Trump is expected to sign a trade agreement with Thailand, push deals with other countries and lobby fellow leaders to favour the US over China on artificial intelligence.
He will also take part in the first leaders’ meeting of the Quad partnership – consisting of the US, Japan, India and Australia – since he returned to the White House in January 2025.
White House officials said the president would be accompanied to Apec by Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX entrepreneur who spent almost $500m (£380m) unsuccessfully supporting Republican candidates in this month’s midterms. The reason for Musk’s presence has not been explained.

item.description:

Canada could work with Chinese automakers if US trade talks fail, says Carney
Ahead of Apec summit, PM says ‘Canada is going to move forward either way’ when asked if Chinese investment was leverage in US negotiations
The prime minister of Canada, Mark Carney, said the country could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with the US president, Donald Trump, failed to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.
Carney’s comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.
“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of US trade actions.”Canada and EU announce new alliance open to like-minded countries

He said on Monday that negotiations with the US remained his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers. A day earlier in Manila, in the Philippines, Carney said any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry.
Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in US negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction.

item.title: Anthony Albanese welcomes Trump-Xi-Putin summit – even as European leaders express reservations
item.description:

Anthony Albanese welcomes Trump-Xi-Putin summit – even as European leaders express reservations
‘We think dialogue is a good thing,’ Australian PM says after German chancellor urges the US to work with Europe for peace in Ukraine
Australia has endorsed this week’s historic summit between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in China, even as European leaders warn that the US president must not make major concessions over the war in Ukraine.
The three-way summit is planned to take place in Shenzhen, where the leaders will gather for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) meeting. The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has warned the talks must not lead to a redistribution of influence among world powers or the abandonment of his country, more than four years into the war sparked by Putin’s full-scale invasion.
Speaking in Manila on Sunday, the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, welcomed the talks taking place but insisted the clear message to Putin was that the war should end.
Albanese, in the Philippines before a meeting of Quad leaders and talks with south-east Asian leaders at the Asean summit, left open the possibility of joining an Apec group photo with Putin if China wished for it to go ahead.

item.title: World leaders head to Asia for back-to-back diplomatic summits
item.description:
China will have the home advantage as it welcomes Donald Trump and others for the Apec leaders’ meeting in its southern technology hub of Shenzhen. Photograph: VCG/Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
China will have the home advantage as it welcomes Donald Trump and others for the Apec leaders’ meeting in its southern technology hub of Shenzhen. Photograph: VCG/Getty Images
World leaders head to Asia for back-to-back diplomatic summits
Tussle for influence as trade, tech and regional security to take centre stage in China, Philippines and Cambodia meetings
World leaders will fly in to Asia for back-to-back high-level summits this week against the backdrop of the tussle for influence between the superpowers China and the US.
Beijing will have the home advantage when it welcomes Donald Trump to its southern technology hub of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders’ meeting. It starts two weeks after the US leader lost midterm elections.
The summit also comes after an awkward-at-best revelation that the head of Nvidia, the US chipmaker that for a long time was the world’s most valuable company, was having an affair with a woman US intelligence suspects was a Chinese spy.
Apec represents more than 60% of global GDP and has primarily promoted free trade and multilateralism. This year’s meeting could be defined, however, by the confirmed trilateral meeting between Trump, the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin of Russia.
The three-way meeting has been likened to a modern-day Yalta, when in 1945 then US president, Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Crimea to carve up Europe after the second world war. However, analysts say a “Yalta 2.0” that issues edicts on Ukraine and Taiwan without their involvement is unlikely.

item.title: Yalta became a byword for betrayal. Will Trump, Xi and Putin enact another carve-up?
item.description:
Russia and US approach potential summit seeking China’s help to extricate them from wars of choice, as Putin hopes to find consensus on new global order

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, is among those who have expressed concern that the world will witness a Yalta 2.0 moment if Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin meet trilaterally, as expected, on the sidelines of the Apec summit in China next week.

It is a truism in diplomacy that if you are not around the table, the risk is that you, or your values, are on the menu and about to be carved up. Many excluded from the summit in Shenzhen, principally Ukraine but also eastern Europe and Baltic countries, Taiwan and even Iran, have reason to be nervous that their sponsors might abandon them in a complex geopolitical trade-off that Putin envisions, and Trump seems to endorse.
